author: Aaron Levie
post_text:
You’re going to be hearing a lot more about the forward deployed engineering motion in AI the coming months and years. Here’s the reason. AI simply is not the same as the software we’re used to implementing for decades. In software, you deliver a stable piece of technology to a customer and they adopt it.

Because the software is deterministic, the customer can rely on “straightforward” documentation, go through standard implementation cycles, and normal change management approaches to adopt the tools.

In AI, you’re delivering something that is constantly evolving both due to the nature of the new capabilities and best practices that are emerging and changing at a faster rate than software. But, the bigger reason is because the underlying models change so much that they can meaningfully change the workflow as a result of their upgrades. At Box, we’ve had customers that have seen multiple step function increases in their use-cases with AI just in a matter of quarters.

It’s very hard if every single customer is responsible for figuring out those gains on their own; for this reason it’s far more logical that vendors can share best practices across thousands of companies more efficiently than every single company can learn and manage these best practices themselves. Further, the learnings from those customers should go right back into the core product as a result.

As we go from chat systems that anyone can relatively easily adopt to agentic systems that require more meaningful efforts to manage and update, the FDE motion (or equivalent) essentially becomes a core competency for anyone deploying AI at scale.

author: Barry O'Reilly
post_text:
Most leaders are experimenting with AI.

Very few are building systems around it.

In Chapter 6 of Artificial Organizations, we explore why AI adoption often breaks down after the first wave of excitement. Leaders try too many tools, automate too early, and end up with fragmented workflows that add complexity instead of reducing it.

This session focuses on a different approach: designing a Personal AI Stack around how you actually work.

The discussion will explore:
- Why high-performing leaders think in systems, not tools
- How to identify the highest-leverage moments in your workflow
- Why traits and tasks should shape your stack before tools do
- How simple workflows compound into better decisions and clearer execution
- The risks of over-automation, tool sprawl, and fragmented information
- What effective AI adoption looks like in real executive work

I will also walk through practical examples from his own workflow and the experience of leaders like Andrew Phillips, CTO of Skyscanner, showing how small experiments evolved into repeatable systems that improved clarity, preparation, follow-through, and decision-making.

This is a session about building infrastructure for how you work day to day.

Because the goal is not to collect AI tools.

It’s to create a system that helps you think clearly, act consistently, and scale your effectiveness over time.

author: Ignacio Martín Prieto
post_text:
We still talk about platforms as infrastructure projects.

But the more important question is whether they reduce cognitive load across the engineering org.

I was reading a recent review on platform engineering and internal developer portals, and one detail stood out:
- the industry has adopted platform teams faster than it has developed evidence for what actually works.

Which honestly explains a lot.

A lot of internal platforms become very sophisticated internally… while still feeling heavy to the teams using them.

Too many workflows.
Too many standards.
Too much process disguised as enablement.

The best platform teams reduce the number of decisions product teams need to make repeatedly.

They create clearer defaults.
Safer paths.
Faster onboarding.
More predictable delivery.
Less coordination overhead between teams.

That is the real leverage.
Not “centralization”.
Not “control”.
Not even “developer productivity” in isolation.

It is organizational scalability.

The interesting shift now is that AI will probably amplify this gap even more.

Because if teams can generate software faster, then clarity, guardrails, architecture consistency, and operational simplicity become more important, not less.

The bottleneck moves from writing code to operating systems coherently.

author: Allen Holub
post_text:
Some of the comments on my last post 👇 remind me that not everyone who reads my posts thinks like an architect, so I apologize for that. I'm making assumptions.

The primary assumption that underlies everything I write is that architecture is all about trade-offs and decisions. There is no such thing as a universal approach that works everywhere. The architect's job is to balance the trade-offs and make hard decisions when there is no "right" path. The answer to "should we do A or B" is always "it depends." There are core principles, of course, but the architect's job is to decide how to realize those principles. When I write about principles, I sometimes forget that some will treat those as directives. They are not.

So, let's take DRY vs WET as an example. The key principle in a microservice context (and context is important) is that external dependencies interfere with the core characteristics of independent deployability and loose coupling, so they should be removed (or at least minimized). That principle touches the design in many places.

For example, inter-service communication via API creates strong dependencies and coupling, so it is generally a bad idea in a microservice context. Pub/sub messaging alleviates the problem (though there is obviously a dependency on the message definition and payload, but that is minimal when the messages reflect domain-level events).

Libraries, which are a bag of APIs, create very strong dependencies. If the library API or behavior changes, all the clients must change as well. So, the rule of thumb (a guideline, not a law of nature) is that it's better to duplicate code than to have that external dependency.

But there is another concern: stability. A stable library (which changes very infrequently, if at all) is relatively safe to use. A volatile library is not. Libraries that contain domain logic are very volatile during development, so they are contraindicated. I do not use them in microservice systems. In fact, I'd wonder why there was a library at all. Why isn't that domain logic encapsulated in an entity or service that's doing domain-level work? Sharing domain logic is always a red flag to me.

Conversely, libraries that contain implementation logic (e.g., a JSON library, an HTML library, or any library that's part of the language release) tend to be very stable, so the coupling is looser and DRY applies.

There are other factors as well. E.g., Libraries that don't have a single responsibility need to be broken up—the principle is "interface segregation". I can't list all of these in one post, however.

The main lesson, however, is: use your brain and think like an architect. There are _always_ exceptions and corner cases.
